name: pwd
summary: Prints the full path of the folder you are currently in. Handy when you get lost after a few cd commands or before running something that depends on location.
exampleExplained: Shows something like /home/deploy/app so you know exactly where commands will run.

name: ls
summary: Lists the files and folders in a directory. The most-used command on any server for seeing what is there.
exampleExplained: -l long format (permissions, owner, size, date), -a includes hidden dotfiles like .env, -h shows sizes as K/M/G.

name: cd
summary: Changes your current directory. With no argument it takes you to your home folder.
exampleExplained: Moves into the app folder. Use cd .. to go up one level and cd ~ (or plain cd) to go home.

name: ls -ltr
summary: A variant of ls that sorts files by modification time. Great for spotting the newest log or the file you just changed.
exampleExplained: -l long listing, -t sort by time (newest first), -r reverse it so the newest files appear at the bottom, right above your prompt.

name: tree
summary: Shows a folder and its subfolders as an indented tree. Often not installed by default; get it with apt install tree.
exampleExplained: -L 2 limits depth to two levels, -I node_modules hides that folder so the output stays readable.

name: man
summary: Opens the manual page for a command, describing every option. Press / to search, q to quit.
exampleExplained: Shows the full manual for tar. Use man -k keyword to search all manual pages by topic.

name: whatis
summary: Prints a one-line description of a command taken from its manual page. A quick way to recall what a command is for.
exampleExplained: Prints a short line like rsync - a fast, versatile, remote file-copying tool.

name: apropos
summary: Searches manual page names and descriptions for a keyword. Useful when you know what you want to do but not the command name.
exampleExplained: Lists every command whose description mentions compress, such as gzip, xz and zip.

name: history
summary: Lists the commands you ran earlier in this shell. You can re-run one with !number or search it interactively with Ctrl+R.
exampleExplained: Shows your last 20 commands. Then !512 would re-run command number 512.

name: clear
summary: Clears the terminal screen so you get a fresh view. Ctrl+L does the same thing.
exampleExplained: Wipes the visible screen; your scrollback history and shell state are unchanged.

name: echo
summary: Prints text or variable values to the screen. Commonly used in scripts and to check environment variables.
exampleExplained: Prints the sentence with $HOME replaced by your home path. Double quotes allow variables to expand.

name: touch
summary: Creates an empty file, or updates the modified time of an existing one without changing its content.
exampleExplained: Creates an empty .env file if missing; if it exists, only its timestamp is refreshed.

name: mkdir
summary: Creates a new directory.
exampleExplained: Makes a folder called logs inside the current directory. Fails if it already exists.

name: mkdir -p
summary: Creates a directory and any missing parent folders in one go, and does not complain if it already exists. Safe to use in scripts.
exampleExplained: -p builds every missing folder in the path and is silent if the path is already there.

name: cp
summary: Copies a file to a new name or location.
exampleExplained: Makes a copy of the example config under a new name, leaving the original untouched.

name: cp -r
summary: Copies a whole directory and everything inside it.
exampleExplained: -r copies recursively; -a goes further and also keeps permissions, ownership and timestamps (archive mode).

name: mv
summary: Moves or renames files and folders. There is no separate rename step; renaming is just moving to a new name.
exampleExplained: Renames app.log to app.log.old. Add -i to be asked before overwriting an existing file.

name: rm
summary: Deletes files permanently. There is no trash bin, so double-check what you type.
exampleExplained: -i asks for confirmation before deleting, a good habit when you are unsure.

name: rm -rf
summary: Deletes a folder and everything inside it without asking. Very dangerous: a wrong path or a stray space can wipe important data, so always check the path first.
exampleExplained: -r removes folder contents recursively, -f never prompts. The ./ makes it clear you mean the folder here. Never run it with sudo on paths like / or a blank variable.

name: rmdir
summary: Removes an empty directory. It refuses if the folder has anything in it, which makes it a safe choice.
exampleExplained: Deletes tmp-build only if it is empty; otherwise it prints an error and does nothing.

name: ln -s
summary: Creates a symbolic link, a shortcut that points to another file or folder. Common for switching app releases or enabling nginx sites.
exampleExplained: -s makes a symlink, -f replaces an existing link, -n treats an existing link to a folder as a file so it is swapped rather than nested.

name: ln
summary: Without -s, creates a hard link: a second name for the same file data. Deleting one name keeps the data alive through the other.
exampleExplained: Both names now point at the same data on disk; editing one shows in the other. Hard links cannot span disks or point to folders.

name: file
summary: Tells you what kind of data a file holds by looking at its content, not its extension.
exampleExplained: Might print PNG image data or gzip compressed data, which helps when a file has the wrong extension.

name: stat
summary: Shows detailed info about a file: size, permissions in number form, owner, and access, modify and change times.
exampleExplained: Prints size, inode, permission bits like 0644, owner and the exact timestamps.

name: basename
summary: Strips the folder path (and optionally a suffix) from a file path, leaving just the file name. Useful in scripts.
exampleExplained: Prints access: the directory part is removed and the .log suffix is dropped.

name: dirname
summary: Returns only the folder part of a path. Often used in scripts to find where the script itself lives.
exampleExplained: Prints /var/log/nginx.

name: realpath
summary: Prints the absolute path of a file, resolving .., . and symlinks.
exampleExplained: Turns the relative path into a full path like /home/deploy/config/app.json.

name: readlink
summary: Shows where a symbolic link points. With -f it follows the whole chain to the final real file.
exampleExplained: -f resolves every link in the chain and prints the final target, e.g. /var/www/releases/v2.

name: mktemp
summary: Creates a temporary file or folder with a unique random name and prints its path. Safer than inventing your own temp names in scripts.
exampleExplained: -d creates a directory instead of a file; its path, like /tmp/tmp.Xa12bC, is stored in the tmpdir variable.

name: truncate
summary: Shrinks or grows a file to a given size. Commonly used to empty a huge log file without deleting it, so the app keeps writing to it.
exampleExplained: -s 0 sets the file size to zero, freeing disk space while keeping the same file open for the running process.

name: install
summary: Copies files while setting permissions and owner in one step. Used in build and deploy scripts instead of cp plus chmod plus chown.
exampleExplained: -m sets mode 755, -o and -g set owner and group, then the file is copied into /usr/local/bin.

name: cat
summary: Prints the whole content of one or more files to the screen. Best for short files; also used to join files together.
exampleExplained: Dumps the file to the terminal. cat a.txt b.txt > both.txt would join two files into one.

name: less
summary: Opens a file in a scrollable viewer that loads quickly even for huge logs. Search with /, jump to end with G, quit with q.
exampleExplained: +F starts in follow mode like tail -f; press Ctrl+C to stop following and scroll, F to resume.

name: more
summary: An older, simpler pager that shows a file one screen at a time. Use less when available; more is still found on minimal systems.
exampleExplained: Space goes to the next page, q quits. It can only scroll forward on many systems.

name: head
summary: Shows the first lines of a file, 10 by default. Good for peeking at CSVs or large files.
exampleExplained: -n 5 prints only the first five lines, e.g. the header and four rows.

name: tail
summary: Shows the last lines of a file, 10 by default. Perfect for checking the latest log entries.
exampleExplained: -n 50 prints the last 50 lines of the log.

name: tail -f
summary: Keeps a file open and prints new lines as they are written. The classic way to watch a Node app log live.
exampleExplained: -f follows new output; capital -F also keeps working if the log is rotated or recreated. Ctrl+C to stop.

name: wc
summary: Counts lines, words and bytes in files or piped input.
exampleExplained: -l prints only the number of lines, a quick way to count requests in a log.

name: nl
summary: Prints a file with line numbers added in front of each line.
exampleExplained: -ba numbers all lines, including blank ones, which matches what your editor shows.

name: xxd
summary: Shows a hex dump of a file, revealing raw bytes. Useful for finding hidden characters like BOMs or Windows line endings.
exampleExplained: Prints byte offsets, hex values and printable text side by side for the first lines.

name: chmod
summary: Changes who can read, write or execute a file using letters: u user, g group, o others, a all.
exampleExplained: u+x adds execute permission for the file owner so you can run ./deploy.sh.

name: chmod numeric
summary: Sets permissions with three digits: read=4, write=2, execute=1, added up for owner, group and others.
exampleExplained: 6 (4+2) owner can read and write, 4 group can read, 0 others get nothing. 755 and 644 are other common choices.

name: ls -l permissions
summary: Reading the permission string from ls -l, like -rwxr-xr--, is key to fixing access problems. First char is type, then three rwx sets.
exampleExplained: -rwxr-xr-- means a regular file; owner can read/write/execute, group read/execute, others read only.

name: chown
summary: Changes the owner (and optionally group) of a file. Usually needs sudo.
exampleExplained: Makes user deploy the owner and www-data the group, written as user:group.

name: chown -R
summary: Changes ownership of a folder and all its contents. A common fix after files were created with sudo.
exampleExplained: -R applies the new owner and group to every file and subfolder in the app.

name: chgrp
summary: Changes only the group that owns a file.
exampleExplained: Gives group ownership of the uploads folder to www-data so the web server group can use it.

name: umask
summary: Shows or sets the default permissions removed from new files. A umask of 022 means new files get 644 and folders get 755.
exampleExplained: New files will be 640 and folders 750 in this shell, so others get no access.

name: sudo
summary: Runs one command as root (or another user) after checking your password. Use it only for commands that really need admin rights.
exampleExplained: Runs the restart as root. Your sudo rights are listed in /etc/sudoers.

name: sudo -u
summary: Runs a command as a specific non-root user. Useful to test whether the app user can read a file or to run the app as that user.
exampleExplained: Tries to read the file as www-data, showing whether that user has permission.

name: su
summary: Switches to another user account in the current terminal. With a dash you also get that user's full login environment.
exampleExplained: Starts a login shell as the deploy user without needing deploy's password, since sudo already made you root.

name: setfacl
summary: Sets access control lists, which give extra users or groups permissions beyond the basic owner/group/others model.
exampleExplained: -m modifies the ACL to give user alice read and write access without changing the owner or group.

name: getfacl
summary: Shows the access control list of a file, including any extra user or group rules set with setfacl.
exampleExplained: Prints owner, group and every ACL entry like user:alice:rw-.

name: chattr
summary: Changes special file attributes on ext filesystems. The immutable flag stops even root from changing or deleting a file.
exampleExplained: +i makes the file immutable; remove it later with chattr -i before editing.

name: lsattr
summary: Lists the special attributes set with chattr, such as i for immutable or a for append-only.
exampleExplained: Shows a flag string; an i in it explains why you cannot edit the file even with sudo.

name: find
summary: Searches a folder tree for files by name, type, size, time and more. Works anywhere, no index needed.
exampleExplained: Searches from the current folder for regular files (-type f) whose names end in .log. Quote the pattern so the shell does not expand it.

name: find -mtime
summary: Finds files by how long ago they were modified, in days. Good for cleaning up old logs or backups.
exampleExplained: -mtime +30 matches files changed more than 30 days ago. -mmin -10 would match files changed in the last 10 minutes.

name: find -size
summary: Finds files bigger or smaller than a size. Perfect when the disk fills up and you need the culprits.
exampleExplained: -size +500M means larger than 500 MB, -xdev stays on one filesystem, 2>/dev/null hides permission errors.

name: find -exec
summary: Runs a command on every file find matches. Lets you delete, compress or change many files at once.
exampleExplained: {} is replaced by matched file names and + passes many at once. Run without -exec first to preview what will be removed.

name: locate
summary: Finds files by name instantly using a prebuilt database. Faster than find but may miss very new files. Install with apt install plocate.
exampleExplained: Prints every indexed path containing nginx.conf in a fraction of a second.

name: updatedb
summary: Rebuilds the database used by locate. It normally runs daily, but you can run it after creating many files.
exampleExplained: Rescans the filesystem so locate can see recently added files.

name: which
summary: Shows the full path of the program that runs when you type a command. Helpful when several versions of node are installed.
exampleExplained: Prints something like /usr/bin/node or a path inside ~/.nvm, showing which node binary wins.

name: whereis
summary: Finds the binary, source and man page locations for a command.
exampleExplained: Lists paths such as /usr/bin/python3 and /usr/share/man/man1/python3.1.gz.

name: type
summary: Tells you how the shell will interpret a name: alias, function, builtin or a file on disk.
exampleExplained: Might print ll is aliased to ls -alF, revealing that ll is an alias rather than a program.

name: grep
summary: Searches text for lines matching a pattern. Works on files or on output piped from another command.
exampleExplained: Prints every line of app.log that contains ERROR. Matching is case-sensitive by default.

name: grep -i -n
summary: Common grep options: ignore case and show line numbers, so you can jump straight to the spot in an editor.
exampleExplained: -i matches Timeout, TIMEOUT and so on; -n prefixes each result with its line number.

name: grep -r
summary: Searches every file inside a folder tree. Great for finding where a function or config value is used.
exampleExplained: -r recurses into folders, -n shows line numbers, --exclude-dir skips node_modules to keep it fast.

name: grep -v
summary: Inverts the match, showing only lines that do NOT contain the pattern. Useful for filtering out noise.
exampleExplained: Prints all log lines except those from health checks.

name: grep -E
summary: Turns on extended regular expressions so you can use |, +, ? and groups without backslashes.
exampleExplained: Matches lines that contain either ERROR or WARN.

name: grep -A -B
summary: Shows lines of context after (-A) or before (-B) each match. Ideal for seeing a stack trace around an error.
exampleExplained: Prints 2 lines before and 5 lines after each match; -C 3 would give 3 on both sides.

name: rg
summary: ripgrep: a very fast recursive search tool that skips files in .gitignore by default. Install with apt install ripgrep.
exampleExplained: Searches src for process.env with line numbers and colors, ignoring node_modules if it is gitignored.

name: fdfind
summary: fd is a simpler, faster alternative to find. On Ubuntu the package is fd-find and the command is fdfind.
exampleExplained: Finds files with the .js extension whose names contain config, skipping hidden and ignored files.

name: command -v
summary: A portable way to check if a command exists, often used in scripts before calling a tool.
exampleExplained: Prints docker's path if installed; otherwise the || part runs and prints the message.

name: ps
summary: Shows a snapshot of running processes. With aux you see every process on the machine, with CPU, memory and the command line.
exampleExplained: a and x include all users' processes and ones without a terminal, u adds user/CPU/memory columns; grep filters to node.

name: top
summary: A live, updating view of processes sorted by CPU use, plus load and memory totals. Press M to sort by memory, q to quit.
exampleExplained: -o %MEM starts top sorted by memory use instead of CPU.

name: htop
summary: A friendlier, colorful version of top with mouse support, tree view and easy killing. Install with apt install htop.
exampleExplained: -u deploy shows only processes owned by the deploy user. F5 toggles tree view, F9 sends a signal.

name: kill
summary: Sends a signal to a process by its PID. By default it sends SIGTERM, which politely asks the program to shut down.
exampleExplained: Asks process 12345 to stop; a Node app can catch SIGTERM to close DB connections cleanly first.

name: kill -9
summary: Sends SIGKILL, which the process cannot catch or ignore. Use only when a normal kill fails, as the app gets no chance to clean up.
exampleExplained: -9 is SIGKILL: the kernel ends the process immediately. Open files and unsaved data are not flushed by the app.

name: pkill
summary: Kills processes by name or other attributes instead of PID.
exampleExplained: -f matches against the full command line, so only the node process running server.js is signaled.

name: pgrep
summary: Finds process IDs by name, without the noise of ps piped to grep.
exampleExplained: -a prints each PID with its full command line, listing every running node process.

name: killall
summary: Kills all processes with an exact program name.
exampleExplained: -s HUP sends the hang-up signal to every nginx process, which many daemons treat as reload config.

name: pidof
summary: Prints the PIDs of a running program given its exact name.
exampleExplained: Outputs the PID(s) of the mongod daemon, or nothing if it is not running.

name: pstree
summary: Shows processes as a tree so you can see which process started which. Great for understanding pm2 or systemd children.
exampleExplained: Shows the process tree for user deploy with -p adding PIDs next to each name.

name: jobs
summary: Lists background or paused jobs started from the current shell.
exampleExplained: -l shows job numbers along with PIDs and their state such as Running or Stopped.

name: bg
summary: Resumes a paused job in the background. Pair it with Ctrl+Z, which pauses the job running in the foreground.
exampleExplained: Continues job 1 in the background so you get your prompt back.

name: fg
summary: Brings a background or paused job back to the foreground so you can interact with it.
exampleExplained: Job 1 takes over the terminal again; Ctrl+C would now stop it.

name: command &
summary: Ending a command with & runs it in the background of the current shell so you can keep typing. It still dies when you log out.
exampleExplained: Runs the build in the background, sending output and errors to build.log; the shell prints the job number and PID.

name: nohup
summary: Runs a command that keeps going after you log out by ignoring the hang-up signal. A quick fix, though systemd or pm2 is better for real services.
exampleExplained: nohup ignores logout, output goes to out.log, & puts it in the background.

name: disown
summary: Detaches a background job from the shell so it is not killed when you close the terminal.
exampleExplained: Removes job 1 from the shell's job list; it keeps running after logout.

name: nice
summary: Starts a command with a lower (or higher) CPU priority. Higher nice values mean the process yields to others.
exampleExplained: Runs the build with niceness 10 so the live app gets CPU first. Only root can use negative values.

name: renice
summary: Changes the priority of a process that is already running.
exampleExplained: Sets process 12345 to niceness 5, lowering its CPU priority.

name: timeout
summary: Runs a command but kills it if it takes longer than a time limit. Useful in scripts and CI to avoid hangs.
exampleExplained: Stops npm test after 30 seconds; the exit code is 124 when the timeout fires.

name: watch
summary: Runs a command again every few seconds and shows the fresh output full screen. Good for watching disk, memory or a queue.
exampleExplained: -n 2 refreshes every 2 seconds. Add -d to highlight what changed between runs.

name: sleep
summary: Pauses for a number of seconds (or m, h). Used in scripts between retries.
exampleExplained: Waits 5 seconds, then checks the health endpoint.

name: time
summary: Measures how long a command takes, showing real (wall clock), user and system CPU time.
exampleExplained: After npm ci finishes, prints real, user and sys times so you can compare install speed.

name: screen
summary: Creates terminal sessions that survive disconnects. Start a long job, detach, log out and reattach later.
exampleExplained: Starts a session named migrate. Ctrl+A then D detaches; screen -r migrate reattaches.

name: tmux
summary: A modern terminal multiplexer: persistent sessions, split panes and windows. Loved for long-running work on servers.
exampleExplained: Creates session deploy. Ctrl+B then D detaches; tmux attach -t deploy brings it back.

name: sort
summary: Sorts lines of text alphabetically by default. Often used with uniq to group and count.
exampleExplained: Prints the lines of names.txt in alphabetical order without changing the file.

name: sort -n -k
summary: Sorts by a chosen column and treats values as numbers, so 100 comes after 20.
exampleExplained: -t, splits on commas, -k3 sorts by column 3, -n compares numerically, -r puts the largest first.

name: uniq
summary: Removes repeated lines that are next to each other, so input usually needs sorting first.
exampleExplained: Sorting puts duplicates side by side, then uniq keeps one copy of each.

name: uniq -c
summary: Counts how many times each line repeats. With sort it builds a quick frequency table.
example: cut -d' ' -f1 access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
exampleExplained: Takes the IP column, groups and counts each IP, and lists the top 10 most frequent visitors.

name: cut
summary: Extracts columns or characters from each line, split by a delimiter.
exampleExplained: -d: uses colon as the separator and -f1 keeps field 1, listing every username.

name: tr
summary: Translates or deletes characters in a stream, like changing case or stripping characters.
exampleExplained: -d deletes every carriage return, turning Windows line endings into Linux ones.

name: sed
summary: A stream editor that applies edits like find-and-replace to text as it flows through.
exampleExplained: s/old/new/g replaces every match on each line and prints the result; the file is not changed.

name: sed -i
summary: Edits a file in place. Powerful for scripted config changes, so keep a backup the first time.
exampleExplained: -i.bak edits .env and saves the original as .env.bak; the regex replaces the whole PORT line.

name: awk
summary: A small language for processing columns of text. Great for pulling fields, filtering rows and doing sums.
exampleExplained: Prints field 1 (client IP) and field 9 (HTTP status) from each nginx log line; fields split on spaces.

name: awk -F
summary: Sets the field separator for awk and lets you add conditions and totals.
exampleExplained: -F, splits on commas; rows with column 3 above 100 are added up and the total is printed at the end.

name: paste
summary: Joins lines from files side by side, or merges many lines into one.
exampleExplained: -s joins all lines of the file into one, -d, puts commas between them: 1,2,3.

name: diff
summary: Compares two files line by line and shows what differs.
exampleExplained: -u prints a unified diff with - for removed and + for added lines, the same style git uses.

name: comm
summary: Compares two sorted files and shows lines unique to each and lines in both.
exampleExplained: -12 hides columns 1 and 2, leaving only lines present in both files.

name: tee
summary: Writes input to a file and to the screen at the same time. Also the standard way to write root-owned files with sudo.
exampleExplained: tee runs as root via sudo and -a appends. A plain sudo echo > file would fail because the redirect is done by your shell.

name: column
summary: Formats text into neat aligned columns, making CSV or command output readable.
exampleExplained: -t builds a table, -s, splits on commas so each field lines up.

name: printf
summary: Prints formatted text with control over spacing and number formats. More predictable than echo in scripts.
exampleExplained: %-10s left-aligns a string in 10 chars, %5d right-aligns a number in 5, \n ends the line.

name: split
summary: Splits a big file into smaller pieces by lines or size. Handy for huge CSV imports or uploads with size limits.
exampleExplained: -l 100000 puts 100k lines in each piece, named part_aa, part_ab and so on.

name: seq
summary: Prints a sequence of numbers, mostly used in loops and quick tests.
exampleExplained: Prints 1 to 5, one per line. seq 0 10 100 counts by tens.

name: jq
summary: A command-line JSON processor: pretty-prints, filters and reshapes JSON. Essential for APIs and logs. Install with apt install jq.
exampleExplained: Pretty-prints the response and outputs the email field of each element in the array.

name: dos2unix
summary: Converts Windows CRLF line endings to Linux LF. Fixes errors like bad interpreter: /bin/bash^M. Install with apt install dos2unix.
exampleExplained: Rewrites deploy.sh in place with Linux line endings so the shebang works.

name: envsubst
summary: Replaces $VAR placeholders in text with environment variable values. Great for templating config files in deploys.
exampleExplained: Every $PORT or ${PORT} in the template becomes 3000 in the output file.

name: ping
summary: Checks if a host is reachable and how long round trips take, using ICMP packets.
exampleExplained: -c 4 sends four packets then stops (on Linux ping runs forever without it) and prints loss and timing.

name: curl
summary: Transfers data to or from URLs. The go-to tool for testing APIs, downloading files and checking web servers.
exampleExplained: -s silent mode hides the progress bar and prints just the response body.

name: curl -I
summary: Fetches only the HTTP response headers. Quick way to check status codes, redirects and caching headers.
exampleExplained: -I sends a HEAD request and prints status line and headers such as content-type.

name: curl POST JSON
summary: Sends a POST request with a JSON body, like Postman in one line.
exampleExplained: -X POST sets the method, -H adds a header, -d supplies the request body.

name: wget
summary: Downloads files from the web, can resume broken downloads and mirror sites.
exampleExplained: -c continues a partially downloaded file instead of starting over.

name: ip addr
summary: Shows network interfaces and their IP addresses. The modern replacement for ifconfig.
exampleExplained: -br prints a brief one-line summary per interface with state and IPs.

name: ip route
summary: Shows the routing table, including the default gateway traffic leaves through.
exampleExplained: Prints which interface and gateway would be used to reach 8.8.8.8.

name: ip link
summary: Shows or changes network interface state, such as bringing a link up or down.
exampleExplained: Lists interfaces with MAC address, MTU and whether they are UP.

name: ss
summary: Shows sockets and listening ports. Use it to see what is running on port 3000 or 27017.
exampleExplained: -t TCP, -u UDP, -l listening only, -p shows process, -n shows numbers instead of names.

name: netstat
summary: The older tool for listing connections and ports, still common in guides. Part of net-tools; ss is the modern choice.
exampleExplained: Same flags as ss: TCP, UDP, listening, process names, numeric ports.

name: hostname
summary: Prints the machine's network name, or its IP addresses with -I.
exampleExplained: -I lists all IP addresses assigned to the machine (Linux-specific flag).

name: dig
summary: Queries DNS records in detail. Essential when a domain is not pointing where you expect. Part of dnsutils.
exampleExplained: Asks for A records of myapp.com; +short prints just the IP addresses.

name: nslookup
summary: A simpler DNS lookup tool, available on most systems.
exampleExplained: Looks up myapp.com using the DNS server 1.1.1.1 instead of the default one.

name: traceroute
summary: Shows each router hop between you and a host, which helps find where traffic slows or stops.
exampleExplained: Prints each hop with its timing; rows of * mean that hop did not reply.

name: mtr
summary: Combines ping and traceroute into a live view of every hop with packet loss. Install with apt install mtr.
exampleExplained: -r report mode, -w wide names, -c 50 sends 50 probes then prints a summary table.

name: nc
summary: netcat: opens raw TCP or UDP connections. Great for testing whether a port is open from a server.
exampleExplained: -z just scans without sending data, -v reports success or failure. Shows if MongoDB's port is reachable.

name: ssh
summary: Logs into a remote server securely or runs a command there. The way you reach Linux servers from your Mac.
exampleExplained: -i picks the private key file; deploy is the user and the IP is the server.

name: ssh -L
summary: Creates a local port forward through SSH, letting you reach a remote service like a private MongoDB from your laptop.
exampleExplained: Your local port 27018 now tunnels to port 27017 on the server; connect Compass to localhost:27018.

name: ssh-keygen
summary: Generates an SSH key pair for passwordless, secure logins.
exampleExplained: -t ed25519 picks a modern key type, -C adds a comment label. Keys go into ~/.ssh by default.

name: ssh-copy-id
summary: Copies your public key to a server's authorized_keys so you can log in with your key.
exampleExplained: Asks for the password once, then installs your public key for future key-based logins.

name: scp
summary: Copies files over SSH between your machine and a server.
exampleExplained: -r copies the folder recursively to the remote path after the colon.

name: rsync
summary: Syncs files locally or over SSH, sending only what changed. Faster and safer than scp for repeated deploys and backups.
exampleExplained: -a keeps permissions and times, -v verbose, -z compresses in transit, --exclude skips node_modules.

name: rsync --delete
summary: Makes the destination an exact mirror by removing files that no longer exist in the source. Preview with --dry-run first.
exampleExplained: --delete removes extra files at the destination; --dry-run only shows what would change. The trailing slash on dist/ means its contents.

name: sftp
summary: An interactive file transfer session over SSH, with commands like ls, get and put.
exampleExplained: Opens an sftp> prompt; get file downloads, put file uploads, exit closes.

name: ssh config
summary: The ~/.ssh/config file lets you define short aliases with host, user, key and port, so long ssh commands become one word.
exampleExplained: Works after adding Host prod with HostName, User and IdentityFile lines to ~/.ssh/config.

name: whois
summary: Shows registration info for a domain or IP: owner org, registrar, expiry date.
exampleExplained: Prints registrar, creation and expiry dates, and name servers for the domain.

name: resolvectl
summary: Shows and controls DNS settings on systems using systemd-resolved, like modern Ubuntu.
exampleExplained: Prints which DNS servers each interface uses. resolvectl query example.com resolves a name.

name: tcpdump
summary: Captures and shows network packets live. Powerful for debugging traffic that never reaches your app.
exampleExplained: -i any listens on all interfaces, -n skips name lookups, port 3000 filters to that port's traffic.

name: apt update
summary: Refreshes the list of available packages from the repositories. Run it before installing or upgrading anything.
exampleExplained: Downloads the latest package lists; it does not install or upgrade anything by itself.

name: apt upgrade
summary: Installs newer versions of all installed packages. Do it regularly for security fixes.
exampleExplained: Upgrades all packages; -y answers yes automatically. Run apt update first.

name: apt install
summary: Installs a package and its dependencies on Debian/Ubuntu.
exampleExplained: Downloads and installs nginx; -y skips the confirmation prompt.

name: apt remove
summary: Uninstalls a package but keeps its configuration files.
exampleExplained: Removes the nginx program; configs in /etc/nginx stay in case you reinstall.

name: apt purge
summary: Uninstalls a package and also deletes its system-wide config files.
exampleExplained: Removes nginx and its config files for a clean slate. Your own data elsewhere is not touched.

name: apt autoremove
summary: Removes dependency packages that nothing needs anymore, freeing space.
exampleExplained: Lists unused dependencies and removes them after confirmation.

name: apt search
summary: Searches available packages by name and description.
exampleExplained: Lists packages related to redis with short descriptions.

name: apt show
summary: Shows details about a package: version, size, dependencies and description.
exampleExplained: Prints the version your repos offer, which is often older than what you want for Node.

name: apt list
summary: Lists packages, filtered by installed or upgradable status.
exampleExplained: Shows packages with newer versions waiting; --installed lists everything installed.

name: apt-cache policy
summary: Shows which version of a package is installed and which repositories offer which versions.
exampleExplained: Prints Installed and Candidate versions plus the repo each comes from, handy after adding NodeSource.

name: apt-mark hold
summary: Pins a package so upgrades skip it. Useful to keep a known-good database version.
exampleExplained: Marks mongodb-org as held; apt upgrade will not touch it until you run apt-mark unhold.

name: dpkg -i
summary: Installs a .deb package file you downloaded. dpkg is the low-level tool under apt.
exampleExplained: Installs the local .deb file. dpkg does not fetch dependencies; if it reports missing ones, run sudo apt -f install (or use apt install ./file.deb).

name: dpkg -l
summary: Lists installed packages with their versions and status.
exampleExplained: Shows nginx-related packages; ii at the start means installed fine.

name: add-apt-repository
summary: Adds an extra package source, such as a PPA, on Ubuntu.
exampleExplained: Registers the PPA so newer Python versions become installable; it refreshes package lists too.

name: snap
summary: Ubuntu's sandboxed package system. Snaps bundle their dependencies and update themselves.
exampleExplained: Installs certbot as a snap; --classic gives it normal system access.

name: dnf
summary: The package manager on Fedora, RHEL, Rocky and Amazon Linux 2023. Same ideas as apt with different names.
exampleExplained: Installs git on a Red Hat family system. dnf upgrade updates everything.

name: update-alternatives
summary: Chooses which version of a program the generic name points to when several are installed, such as python3 or java.
exampleExplained: Shows a numbered menu of installed editors and sets the system default.

name: df
summary: Shows how much space is used and free on each mounted filesystem. The first thing to run when a server says no space left on device.
exampleExplained: -h prints sizes in human units like 20G. Look at the Use% column for the root (/) filesystem.

name: du
summary: Shows how much disk space files and folders use. Use it to find what is eating your disk.
exampleExplained: -s gives one total for the folder, -h prints human-readable sizes.

name: du sorted
summary: Combining du with sort lists the biggest folders first, the fastest way to track down disk hogs.
exampleExplained: Sizes each folder directly under /var, sort -hr orders human sizes largest first, head shows the top 10.

name: ncdu
summary: An interactive disk usage browser. Navigate folders with arrow keys to see what is big, and delete with d. Install with apt install ncdu.
exampleExplained: -x stays on the root filesystem so other mounts are not scanned.

name: lsblk
summary: Lists disks and partitions as a tree with sizes and mount points. Good for spotting a newly attached cloud volume.
exampleExplained: -f adds filesystem type, label, UUID and mount point for each device.

name: blkid
summary: Prints filesystem type and UUID of block devices. The UUID is what you put in /etc/fstab.
exampleExplained: Shows UUID and TYPE (e.g. ext4) of that volume.

name: mount
summary: Attaches a filesystem to a folder so its files become accessible. Without arguments it lists current mounts.
exampleExplained: Makes the volume's contents appear under /mnt/data. The folder must exist first.

name: umount
summary: Detaches a mounted filesystem. It fails if a process is still using it.
exampleExplained: Unmounts the volume. If it says target is busy, check with lsof +D /mnt/data.

name: findmnt
summary: Shows mounted filesystems as a clear tree, and can verify your fstab file.
exampleExplained: Checks /etc/fstab for mistakes before a reboot, which could otherwise leave the server unbootable.

name: fdisk
summary: Views and edits disk partition tables. Editing is destructive, so double-check the device name.
exampleExplained: -l only lists disks and partitions; it changes nothing.

name: mkfs.ext4
summary: Creates a new ext4 filesystem on a partition or volume. This ERASES everything on that device.
exampleExplained: Formats the new empty volume as ext4 with label data. Confirm the device with lsblk first.

name: fsck
summary: Checks and repairs a filesystem. Run it only on unmounted filesystems.
exampleExplained: -n checks without fixing anything, a safe first look. Without -n it may ask to repair.

name: resize2fs
summary: Grows (or shrinks) an ext4 filesystem, for example after enlarging a cloud disk.
exampleExplained: Expands the filesystem to fill its partition. Grow the partition first, often with growpart.

name: growpart
summary: Extends a partition to use free space after a cloud disk was resized. Part of cloud-guest-utils.
exampleExplained: Grows partition 1 of the disk; follow with resize2fs to grow the filesystem.

name: mkswap
summary: Prepares a file or partition to be used as swap space.
exampleExplained: Writes swap headers to /swapfile. Create it first with fallocate and chmod 600.

name: swapon
summary: Enables swap space, or lists active swap. Small servers running npm builds often need some swap.
exampleExplained: Lists active swap files or partitions with their size and usage.

name: fallocate
summary: Quickly reserves disk space for a file. Commonly used to create a swap file.
exampleExplained: -l 2G makes a 2 GB file instantly without writing zeros.

name: dd
summary: Copies raw data block by block. Used for disk images and test files, but a wrong of= target can wipe a disk.
exampleExplained: Writes 100 blocks of 1 MB zeros into test.img. if= is input, of= is output; never point of= at a disk by mistake.

name: sync
summary: Forces data still in memory to be written to disk. Use before removing a USB drive or after big copies.
exampleExplained: Flushes pending writes so data is safely on disk.

name: lvs
summary: Lists LVM logical volumes. LVM lets you resize and combine disks more flexibly than plain partitions.
exampleExplained: Shows each logical volume, its volume group and size.

name: whoami
summary: Prints the name of the user you are acting as. Useful after sudo or su to confirm who you are.
exampleExplained: Prints e.g. deploy, or root inside a sudo shell.

name: id
summary: Shows your user ID, group ID and all groups you belong to. Key for debugging permission errors.
exampleExplained: Prints uid, gid and groups of deploy, e.g. showing whether it is in the docker or www-data group.

name: groups
summary: Lists the groups a user belongs to.
exampleExplained: Prints group names like deploy sudo www-data.

name: who
summary: Shows who is logged in right now and from where.
exampleExplained: Lists logged-in users, their terminals, login times and source IPs.

name: w
summary: Shows logged-in users and what they are running, plus uptime and load averages.
exampleExplained: Each row shows the user, where they came from, idle time and their current command.

name: last
summary: Lists recent logins and reboots from the login history.
exampleExplained: Shows the last 10 logins with times and IPs; reboot lines show when the server restarted.

name: adduser
summary: Creates a new user interactively on Debian/Ubuntu, setting up a home folder and password. Friendlier than useradd.
exampleExplained: Creates user deploy with /home/deploy and asks for a password and optional details.

name: useradd
summary: The low-level command to create users, available on every distro. Good for scripts.
exampleExplained: -m creates a home folder, -s sets the shell, -G adds the user to the sudo group.

name: usermod -aG
summary: Adds an existing user to extra groups. Forgetting -a removes them from all other groups, a classic mistake.
exampleExplained: -a appends, -G docker names the group. The user must log out and in again for it to apply.

name: userdel
summary: Deletes a user account.
exampleExplained: -r also deletes the user's home folder and mail spool. Back up anything needed first.

name: passwd
summary: Changes a user's password. Without a username it changes your own.
exampleExplained: Sets a new password for deploy. passwd -l deploy would lock the password login.

name: groupadd
summary: Creates a new group.
exampleExplained: Creates the developers group; add people to it with usermod -aG.

name: getent
summary: Looks up entries in system databases like users, groups and hosts, including ones from LDAP.
exampleExplained: Prints the passwd line for deploy: uid, gid, home folder and shell.

name: visudo
summary: Safely edits the sudoers file, checking syntax before saving so you cannot lock yourself out.
exampleExplained: Edits a separate drop-in file; a line like deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/systemctl restart myapp allows one command.

name: uname
summary: Prints system information such as kernel version and CPU architecture.
exampleExplained: -a prints everything: kernel name, hostname, kernel release, architecture (x86_64 or aarch64).

name: /etc/os-release
summary: Reading this file tells you which distro and version you are on, which decides the right install instructions.
exampleExplained: Shows NAME, VERSION_ID and VERSION_CODENAME, like Ubuntu 24.04 noble.

name: lsb_release
summary: Prints distribution info on Ubuntu and Debian.
exampleExplained: -a shows distributor, description, release number and codename.

name: uptime
summary: Shows how long the system has been running and the load averages over 1, 5 and 15 minutes.
exampleExplained: A load near your CPU core count means the machine is fully busy; much higher means work is queuing.

name: date
summary: Shows or formats the current date and time. Often used to timestamp file names in scripts.
exampleExplained: Formats the date like 2026-10-05_1430, ideal for backup file names.

name: timedatectl
summary: Shows and sets the system clock, time zone and NTP sync status.
exampleExplained: Sets the time zone to UTC, which keeps logs consistent across servers.

name: hostnamectl
summary: Shows or changes the system hostname and some machine info.
exampleExplained: Sets a permanent hostname so the server is easy to recognize in prompts and logs.

name: systemctl status
summary: Shows whether a service is running, its PID, memory use and recent log lines.
exampleExplained: Shows active (running) or failed, plus the last few log lines to explain why.

name: systemctl restart
summary: Starts, stops or restarts a service managed by systemd.
exampleExplained: Stops and starts myapp. Use start, stop or reload in the same way; reload rereads config without stopping.

name: systemctl enable
summary: Makes a service start automatically at boot. --now also starts it immediately.
exampleExplained: Enables nginx at boot and starts it right away. disable turns auto-start off.

name: systemctl list-units
summary: Lists units systemd knows about, filtered by type or state. Helps find failing services.
exampleExplained: Shows only services that are in the failed state.

name: systemd unit file
summary: A small .service file lets systemd run your Node app, restart it on crash and start it on boot.
exampleExplained: In it, ExecStart=/usr/bin/node /var/www/myapp/server.js, User=deploy and Restart=always define how the app runs.

name: systemctl daemon-reload
summary: Tells systemd to reread unit files after you create or edit them.
exampleExplained: Run it after editing myapp.service, then restart the service so changes apply.

name: journalctl
summary: Reads logs collected by systemd, including stdout of services you run with systemd.
exampleExplained: -u filters to the myapp unit, --since limits to the last hour.

name: journalctl -f
summary: Follows the systemd journal live, like tail -f for service logs.
exampleExplained: -f follows new entries, -n 50 first shows the last 50 lines.

name: dmesg
summary: Shows kernel messages: hardware events, disk errors and the out-of-memory killer.
exampleExplained: -T shows readable timestamps; the grep reveals if the OOM killer stopped your Node app.

name: crontab -e
summary: Edits your scheduled jobs. Each line has five time fields (minute hour day month weekday) and a command.
exampleExplained: Opens your crontab; a line like 0 2 * * * /home/deploy/backup.sh runs the script daily at 02:00.

name: crontab -l
summary: Lists your current scheduled cron jobs.
exampleExplained: -l lists, -u deploy shows that user's crontab instead of yours.

name: at
summary: Schedules a one-time command for later, unlike cron which repeats.
exampleExplained: Queues the restart to run once at 3 AM. atq lists pending jobs.

name: systemctl list-timers
summary: Lists systemd timers, the modern alternative to cron, with their next and last run times.
exampleExplained: Shows every timer, like apt-daily or logrotate, and when it runs next.

name: shutdown
summary: Powers off or reboots the system, optionally after a delay with a warning to users.
exampleExplained: -r reboots in 5 minutes and broadcasts the message. shutdown -c cancels.

name: reboot
summary: Restarts the machine immediately.
exampleExplained: Reboots now. Check that services are enabled first so they come back up.

name: env
summary: Prints all environment variables, or runs a command with a modified environment.
exampleExplained: Runs node with NODE_ENV set only for that one command.

name: printenv
summary: Prints the value of one environment variable or all of them.
exampleExplained: Shows the folders the shell searches for programs, separated by colons.

name: lscpu
summary: Shows CPU details: model, number of cores and threads, architecture.
exampleExplained: Look at CPU(s) to decide how many Node cluster workers to run.

name: modprobe
summary: Loads or removes kernel modules along with their dependencies.
exampleExplained: Loads the module now; add it to /etc/modules-load.d to load at boot.

name: sysctl
summary: Reads or changes kernel settings at runtime, like network buffers or file limits.
exampleExplained: -w writes a value; put it in /etc/sysctl.d/*.conf to keep it after reboot.

name: logrotate
summary: Rotates, compresses and deletes old log files on a schedule so they do not fill the disk.
exampleExplained: -d is debug mode: it shows what would happen without rotating anything.

name: systemd-analyze
summary: Shows how long boot took and which services slowed it down.
exampleExplained: Lists services ordered by how long they took to start.

name: tar -czf
summary: Creates a gzip-compressed tar archive, the standard way to bundle a folder on Linux.
exampleExplained: -c create, -z gzip compress, -f names the archive file. The result holds the whole uploads folder.

name: tar -xzf
summary: Extracts a .tar.gz archive.
exampleExplained: -x extract, -z gunzip, -f archive name, -C sets the folder to extract into (it must exist).

name: tar -tzf
summary: Lists what is inside a .tar.gz without extracting it. Always worth a look before unpacking.
exampleExplained: -t lists the contents; head shows the first 10 entries.

name: tar exclude
summary: Leaves out folders like node_modules or .git when creating an archive.
exampleExplained: Each --exclude skips matching paths, keeping the archive small.

name: gzip
summary: Compresses a file into .gz, replacing the original.
exampleExplained: -k keeps the original file next to the new access.log.gz.

name: gunzip
summary: Decompresses a .gz file.
exampleExplained: Restores access.log and removes the .gz file.

name: zcat
summary: Prints the contents of a .gz file without decompressing it to disk. Pairs well with grep on rotated logs.
exampleExplained: Reads the compressed log and searches it in one go. zgrep does the same in one command.

name: xz
summary: Compresses with high ratio, smaller than gzip and bzip2 but slower.
exampleExplained: -T0 uses all CPU cores, -k keeps the original. Output is dump.sql.xz.

name: zstd
summary: A fast modern compressor with a great speed-to-size ratio. Install with apt install zstd.
exampleExplained: -19 is a high compression level; makes dump.sql.zst. unzstd decompresses.

name: zip
summary: Creates .zip archives, handy when sharing with Windows or macOS users.
exampleExplained: -r adds the folder and everything inside it.

name: unzip
summary: Extracts .zip archives. Install with apt install unzip if missing.
exampleExplained: -d sets the target folder. unzip -l site.zip lists contents without extracting.

name: pipe |
summary: The pipe sends the output of one command into the input of the next, letting you chain small tools into powerful one-liners.
exampleExplained: ps output goes to grep, which keeps node lines, and wc -l counts them.

name: redirection > >>
summary: Redirection sends output to a file instead of the screen. > overwrites the file, >> appends to it.
exampleExplained: Appends the script's output to seed.log rather than replacing its contents.

summary: Redirects error output (stream 2) to wherever normal output (stream 1) goes, so both land in the same file.
exampleExplained: Sends stdout to app.log, then points stderr at the same place. Order matters: put 2>&1 after the file.

name: /dev/null
summary: A special file that throws away anything written to it. Used to silence output you do not need.
exampleExplained: Hides the error message if there is no crontab, then prints a friendly line instead.

name: && and ||
summary: && runs the next command only if the previous one succeeded; || runs it only if it failed. Basic flow control on one line.
example: npm ci && npm run build || echo "build failed"
exampleExplained: Builds only if install succeeded; if either step fails, the message is printed.

name: export
summary: Makes a variable available to programs started from this shell, like process.env in Node.
exampleExplained: Sets NODE_ENV for this shell and every command it launches. Add it to ~/.bashrc to keep it.

name: alias
summary: Creates a shortcut name for a longer command. Put aliases in ~/.bashrc to keep them.
exampleExplained: Typing ll now runs ls -lah. Run alias alone to list current aliases.

name: source
summary: Runs a script inside the current shell, so variables and functions it sets stay available. Used to reload ~/.bashrc.
exampleExplained: Applies new aliases or PATH changes without opening a new terminal. A dot (. ~/.bashrc) does the same.

name: shebang
summary: The first line of a script, starting with #!, tells Linux which interpreter runs it. The file also needs execute permission.
exampleExplained: env finds bash in the PATH. After chmod +x script.sh you can run it as ./script.sh.

name: variables
summary: Shell variables hold text. Assign with no spaces around =, read with $NAME, and quote them to keep spaces intact.
exampleExplained: Spaces around = would break the assignment; quoting "$APP_DIR" avoids surprises with spaces in paths.

summary: Command substitution runs a command and puts its output in place, like a template literal for shell output.
exampleExplained: The date command runs first and its output is inserted into the echoed text.

summary: Holds the exit code of the last command: 0 means success, anything else means failure.
exampleExplained: Prints 0 if tests passed, or a non-zero code if they failed.

name: read
summary: Reads a line of input from the user or a file into variables.
exampleExplained: -p shows a prompt, -r keeps backslashes literal; the reply is stored in $answer.

name: test [ ]
summary: Checks conditions such as whether a file exists or two strings match. [ ] is another name for test.
exampleExplained: -f is true if .env is a regular file; if it is missing, the example is copied in.

summary: Bash's improved test with safer quoting, pattern matching and && / || inside.
exampleExplained: == with a glob on the right matches any branch starting with release/.

name: if
summary: Runs commands only when a condition (any command's exit status) succeeds.
example: if systemctl is-active --quiet myapp; then echo up; else echo down; fi
exampleExplained: is-active returns 0 when the service runs, so the then branch prints up.

name: for loop
summary: Repeats commands for each item in a list, such as files or server names.
example: for f in *.log; do gzip "$f"; done
exampleExplained: Loops over every .log file in the folder and compresses each one.

name: while read loop
summary: Processes a file or command output line by line, safely handling spaces.
example: while IFS= read -r host; do ssh "$host" uptime; done < servers.txt
exampleExplained: Reads each line of servers.txt into $host and runs uptime there. IFS= and -r keep each line exactly as written.

name: case
summary: Chooses between branches by matching a value against patterns. Cleaner than many ifs for command arguments.
example: case "$1" in start) npm start;; stop) pkill -f server.js;; *) echo "usage";; esac
exampleExplained: Matches the first script argument; * catches anything else. Each branch ends with ;;.

name: functions
summary: Groups commands under a name so a script can reuse them. Arguments arrive as $1, $2 and so on.
exampleExplained: Defines log, which prints a timestamp and all its arguments ($*). Then calls it.

name: set -euo pipefail
summary: Strict mode for bash scripts: stop on errors, on unset variables and on failures inside pipes. Put it near the top of deploy scripts.
exampleExplained: -e exits on any failing command, -u errors on unset variables, -o pipefail makes a pipe fail if any part fails.

name: bash -x
summary: Runs a script printing each command before it executes, which makes debugging much easier.
exampleExplained: Every command is printed with a + prefix and variables expanded, so you see exactly what ran.

name: heredoc <<EOF
summary: Feeds a block of multi-line text into a command, useful for writing config files from scripts.
exampleExplained: Everything up to the EOF line becomes input to cat, which writes it to .env. Variables inside are expanded.

name: xargs
summary: Turns input lines into arguments for another command. Useful when a command does not read from a pipe.
exampleExplained: -print0 and -0 separate names with null bytes, so file names with spaces are handled safely.

name: xargs -P
summary: Runs several copies of a command in parallel, speeding up batch jobs.
exampleExplained: -n1 passes one URL per call, -P4 runs four downloads at once, curl -O saves each file.

name: trap
summary: Runs cleanup code when a script exits or receives a signal, such as deleting temp files.
exampleExplained: Whenever the script ends, even on error, the temp folder is removed.

name: getopts
summary: Parses short options like -v or -e prod in your own scripts.
example: while getopts "e:v" opt; do case $opt in e) ENV=$OPTARG;; v) VERBOSE=1;; esac; done
exampleExplained: e: means -e takes a value (in $OPTARG); v is a simple on/off flag.

name: shift
summary: Drops the first script argument and moves the others down one place. Handy when looping over arguments.
exampleExplained: Prints the first argument, then shifts, so $1 now holds what was the second.

name: exec
summary: Replaces the current shell with a command, so it gets the same PID. Common at the end of Docker entrypoint scripts.
exampleExplained: The shell is replaced by node, so signals like SIGTERM reach node directly.

name: shellcheck
summary: A linter for shell scripts that catches quoting bugs and common mistakes, like ESLint for bash. Install with apt install shellcheck.
exampleExplained: Prints warnings with codes such as SC2086 (unquoted variable) and suggests fixes.

name: ulimit
summary: Shows or sets per-process resource limits, like the maximum number of open files. Busy Node servers can hit too many open files.
exampleExplained: Prints the open file limit for this shell. ulimit -n 65535 raises it for the session if allowed.

name: free
summary: Shows total, used and available memory and swap. Look at the available column, not free.
exampleExplained: -h uses readable units. Linux uses spare RAM for cache, so low free with high available is normal.

name: nproc
summary: Prints the number of CPU cores available. Handy for choosing worker counts in scripts.
exampleExplained: Runs make with one job per core.

name: vmstat
summary: Reports memory, swap, CPU and I/O activity over time, showing whether a box is CPU, memory or disk bound.
exampleExplained: Prints a line every 2 seconds, 5 times. High si/so means swapping; high wa means waiting on disk.

name: iostat
summary: Shows disk read/write rates and how busy each disk is. Part of sysstat.
exampleExplained: -x extended stats, -z hides idle devices, 2 refreshes every 2 seconds. %util near 100 means the disk is saturated.

name: sar
summary: Collects and reports historical system activity so you can see what happened during last night's slowdown.
exampleExplained: -u shows CPU use, -f reads the saved data file for day 05.

name: iotop
summary: Shows which processes are doing the most disk I/O, like top for disks.
exampleExplained: -o shows only processes actually doing I/O right now.

name: lsof
summary: Lists open files, including network sockets. On Linux everything is a file, so this reveals a lot.
exampleExplained: Counts files the process has open; a number that keeps growing hints at a file or socket leak.

name: lsof -i
summary: Shows which process is using a network port. The fix for EADDRINUSE: address already in use.
exampleExplained: Lists the process listening on or connected to port 3000, with its PID.

name: fuser
summary: Shows which processes use a file, folder or port, and can kill them.
exampleExplained: -v shows user, PID and command using TCP port 3000.

name: strace
summary: Traces the system calls a process makes. Shows exactly which files it opens or where it hangs.
exampleExplained: -p attaches to a running process, -f follows child threads, -e trace=openat shows only file opens.

name: ldd
summary: Lists the shared libraries a binary needs. Useful when a native npm module fails to load.
exampleExplained: Prints each library and where it was found; not found lines point to missing system packages.

name: /proc
summary: A virtual folder exposing live kernel and process info as files.
exampleExplained: Shows MemTotal, MemFree and MemAvailable straight from the kernel. /proc/<pid>/ has per-process details.

name: perf
summary: Linux's built-in profiler. Finds which functions burn CPU, even inside Node with the right flags.
exampleExplained: Shows a live list of the hottest functions across the system.

name: iftop
summary: Shows network bandwidth use per connection in real time.
exampleExplained: Displays which remote hosts send or receive the most traffic on eth0.

name: ufw
summary: Uncomplicated Firewall: Ubuntu's simple front end for firewall rules. Allow SSH before enabling it so you do not lock yourself out.
example: sudo ufw allow OpenSSH && sudo ufw enable
exampleExplained: Allows SSH first, then turns the firewall on. ufw status verbose shows the rules.

name: ufw allow
summary: Opens a port or service through the firewall, optionally only from certain IPs.
example: sudo ufw allow from 10.0.0.0/24 to any port 27017
exampleExplained: Allows MongoDB's port only from the private subnet, keeping it closed to the internet.

name: iptables
summary: The classic low-level Linux firewall tool. Many systems now use nftables underneath, but iptables commands are everywhere.
exampleExplained: -L lists rules, -n shows numeric addresses, -v adds packet counters.

name: nft
summary: The nftables tool, the modern replacement for iptables on current distros.
exampleExplained: Prints all current firewall tables, chains and rules.

name: fail2ban-client
summary: Controls fail2ban, which bans IPs after repeated failed logins. Install with apt install fail2ban.
exampleExplained: Shows how many IPs are currently banned by the sshd jail.

name: sha256sum
summary: Calculates a SHA-256 checksum to verify a download was not corrupted or tampered with.
exampleExplained: -c checks files against the listed hashes; --ignore-missing skips entries for files you did not download.

name: md5sum
summary: Computes an MD5 hash. Fine for spotting accidental changes, but not secure against tampering.
exampleExplained: Prints a hash; compare it after copying to confirm the file arrived intact.

name: base64
summary: Encodes data to base64 text or decodes it. Common with Kubernetes secrets and basic auth. It is encoding, not encryption.
exampleExplained: -n stops echo adding a newline, which would change the result. base64 -d decodes.

name: openssl rand
summary: Generates cryptographically random data, perfect for secrets like JWT keys.
exampleExplained: Prints 32 random bytes as 64 hex characters.

name: openssl s_client
summary: Connects to a TLS server so you can inspect its certificate. Great for SSL errors.
exampleExplained: -servername sends SNI so you get the right certificate; /dev/null closes the session right away.

name: openssl x509
summary: Reads and displays certificate details such as issuer and expiry date.
exampleExplained: -noout hides the encoded cert, -dates prints notBefore and notAfter.

name: certbot
summary: Gets and renews free Let's Encrypt TLS certificates, and can configure nginx for HTTPS.
exampleExplained: --nginx edits the nginx config for you, -d sets the domain.

name: gpg
summary: Encrypts, decrypts and signs files. Also used to verify signed packages.
exampleExplained: -c encrypts with a passphrase, creating secrets.txt.gpg. gpg -d decrypts it.

name: shred
summary: Overwrites a file several times before deleting it so it is hard to recover. Less effective on SSDs and journaling filesystems.
exampleExplained: -n 3 overwrites three times, -u deletes the file afterwards.

name: sudo -l
summary: Lists which commands your user may run with sudo. Good for auditing access.
exampleExplained: Prints allowed commands, such as (ALL) ALL or a specific list.

name: chmod 600 keys
summary: SSH refuses private keys and config readable by others. Setting tight permissions on ~/.ssh fixes unprotected private key file errors.
exampleExplained: 700 lets only you use the folder; 600 lets only you read and write the key.

name: auth.log
summary: On Ubuntu, /var/log/auth.log records logins, sudo use and SSH attempts. Checking it reveals brute-force attacks.
exampleExplained: Shows the latest failed SSH password attempts with their source IPs.

name: nmap
summary: Scans hosts for open ports and services. Only scan machines you own or have permission to test.
exampleExplained: -sT does a TCP connect scan, -p checks ports 1 to 1000, showing what is exposed.

name: setuid search
summary: Finding files with the setuid bit helps audit programs that run as their owner, often root.
exampleExplained: -perm -4000 matches files with setuid set; -xdev stays on one filesystem.

name: aa-status
summary: Shows the state of AppArmor, the Ubuntu security module that restricts what programs can access.
exampleExplained: Lists loaded profiles and which processes are confined in enforce or complain mode.

name: inotifywait
summary: Waits for file system events like changes or new files, so scripts can react instantly. Part of inotify-tools.
exampleExplained: -m keeps monitoring, -e close_write fires when a file finishes being written.

name: flock
summary: Uses a lock file so only one copy of a script runs at a time. Prevents overlapping cron jobs.
exampleExplained: -n gives up immediately if another run holds the lock instead of waiting.

name: logger
summary: Writes a message to the system log from scripts, so it shows up in journalctl.
exampleExplained: -t sets the tag; view with journalctl -t deploy.

name: pv
summary: Shows a progress bar for data flowing through a pipe. Install with apt install pv.
exampleExplained: pv shows speed, percent done and time left while the file streams to the next command.

name: socat
summary: A Swiss army knife for relaying data between sockets, files and ports, more flexible than nc.
exampleExplained: Listens on 8080 and forwards each connection to port 3000; fork handles many clients.

name: ionice
summary: Sets disk I/O priority so heavy jobs like backups do not slow the live app.
exampleExplained: -c3 is the idle class: tar only uses the disk when nothing else needs it.

name: systemd-run
summary: Runs a command as a temporary systemd unit, with resource limits and journal logging.
exampleExplained: --scope runs it in the foreground within its own cgroup; -p MemoryMax caps memory at 500 MB.

name: unshare
summary: Runs a program in new Linux namespaces, the building block of containers.
exampleExplained: Starts bash in its own PID namespace; inside it, ps shows bash as PID 1.

name: nsenter
summary: Enters the namespaces of another process, such as a running container, to debug from the inside.
exampleExplained: -t picks the target PID, -n joins its network namespace, then ss shows that container's listening ports.

name: chroot
summary: Runs a command with a different folder treated as the root /. Used for system rescue and simple isolation.
exampleExplained: Opens a shell where / is /mnt/rescue, e.g. to repair a broken system from a live disk.
